checks.title: A provider firewall is attached and in force
checks.rationale: A cloud provider's network firewall drops traffic before it reaches the host and before Docker's iptables rules, so it still protects a published container port or a host firewall that was switched off by mistake. This check reads the provider's firewall over its API (opt in with --provider, read only credentials) for each public address of the host. An OVH Edge Network Firewall that has rules but is disabled only filters while OVH switches it on during a detected attack, which is a choice some owners make on purpose, so it is a warning, not a failure. Without --provider this check reports one skip row that says how to enable the module and the other PFW checks leave no row; when the API could not be asked, every PFW check is unknown with the reason.
checks.verify: Hetzner: Cloud Console, Firewalls, check the server is listed under Resources and the status is applied. OVH: Control Panel, Bare Metal Cloud, Network, IP, Edge Network Firewall, check it is enabled for the address
checks.fix: Create a provider firewall that allows only the ports your ingress needs and attach it to this server (Hetzner) or enable the Edge Network Firewall for this address (OVH)
checks.breaks: A provider firewall without a rule for a port drops that traffic: add rules for SSH and every service before attaching it, and on OVH the replies the host needs (see PFW-007).

checks.title: Inbound traffic is denied by default at the provider
checks.rationale: A firewall that only lists what to block leaves every new service open. On a stateless firewall, a permit that matches only a source port (TCP from source port 443, say) also opens every port to a sender that picks that port, so it fails this check for TCP; UDP source port rules are judged in PFW-003. A Hetzner Cloud Firewall drops inbound traffic no rule permits as soon as it is attached. The OVH Edge Network Firewall is the opposite: a packet no rule matches is allowed, and only a final rule that denies every IPv4 packet makes it default deny.
checks.verify: OVH: the rule list of the address ends with a deny rule for protocol IPv4 from any source (OVH's own example uses sequence 19)
checks.fix: OVH: add a last rule (sequence 19) that denies protocol IPv4 from any source, after the permit rules for your services and for return traffic
checks.breaks: Without the return traffic rules of PFW-007 in front of it, a final deny drops the replies to every connection the host opens.

checks.title: No provider rule allows all UDP from anywhere
checks.rationale: UDP has no handshake, so a rule that allows every UDP port from anywhere exposes every UDP service on the host, including ones bound by mistake (DNS resolvers, memcached, game servers) and amplification targets. A wide UDP range is a warning. On a stateless firewall a rule that matches only a source port (OVH's example permits UDP from source port 53) also lets any sender reach every UDP port by choosing that source port; it is reported as a warning, because it is the provider's own advice for DNS replies.
checks.verify: List the inbound UDP rules of the provider firewall and look for a missing port, a range of 1000 ports or more, or a source port with no destination port
checks.fix: Allow only the UDP ports your services use; on OVH, give source port rules a destination port range too where the service allows it (the ephemeral range 32768 to 60999 for replies)
checks.breaks: Removing a UDP rule a service relies on (WireGuard, Tailscale direct connections, QUIC) cuts that service off or slows it down.

checks.title: Every port the provider allows has a service behind it
checks.rationale: A provider rule for a port nothing listens on is either stale (the service moved or was removed, and the next thing to bind that port is exposed without anyone deciding so) or points at a service that is down. Ports a container publishes count as served. When the listening sockets could not be read the result is info, never a verdict.
checks.verify: ss -tulnp, and compare with the provider firewall's permitted ports
checks.fix: Delete the provider rules for ports nothing should serve, or start the service that should be there
checks.breaks: A service that only runs now and then (a backup target, a seasonal game server) loses its rule; keep those rules on purpose.

checks.title: SSH is not open to anywhere at the provider
checks.rationale: SSH open to the whole internet at the provider draws constant brute force traffic and exposes every future sshd flaw. A permit from a source of /8 or wider counts as anywhere; a deny only counts against anywhere when its source is empty, 0.0.0.0/0 or ::ffff:0.0.0.0/96. Like NET-003, this is a failure when Tailscale offers a private path and a warning otherwise. The sshd ports come from the listeners (port 22 when they could not be read).
checks.verify: List the provider firewall's inbound TCP rules for the sshd ports and their sources
checks.fix: Allow SSH at the provider only from the addresses you administer from (a panel, a bastion, your office), or close it there and reach SSH over the tailnet
checks.breaks: Restricting SSH before another way in works locks you out; most providers still give a console in their web panel for that case.

checks.title: IPv6 is covered by the provider or the host firewall
checks.rationale: A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters IPv4 and IPv6 with one rule list. The OVH Edge Network Firewall filters IPv4 only, so a host with a global IPv6 address is open on IPv6 as far as it goes, and the host firewall is the only layer there. This check fails when the host has a global IPv6 address that neither the provider nor a host firewall filters.
checks.verify: ip -6 addr show scope global; and the host firewall's IPv6 rules (ufw status verbose shows (v6) rules)
checks.fix: Keep a host firewall that denies incoming IPv6 by default (UFW with IPV6=yes), or remove the global IPv6 address if nothing uses it
checks.breaks: Removing the IPv6 address breaks clients that reach the host over IPv6 only.

checks.title: A stateless provider firewall lets return traffic in
checks.rationale: A stateless firewall (OVH Edge Network Firewall) does not know which packets are replies. With a final deny rule, replies to everything the host starts (package downloads, DNS, time sync, a Cloudflare Tunnel) are dropped unless rules let them in first, which can cut the host off. A deny that comes before any rule permitting established TCP is a failure. Here a dropped reply is the finding, so a deny counts from a source of /8 or wider (or one that does not parse) and a permit only from an empty source or 0.0.0.0/0. Missing UDP replies for DNS (source port 53), time sync (source port 123, when NTP is on) and a Cloudflare Tunnel's QUIC (source port 7844) are warnings, because the provider's own resolvers and time servers may sit inside its network, where the firewall does not filter, and whether QUIC passes the provider's edge is not settled. Stateful firewalls (Hetzner) skip this check.
checks.verify: OVH: the rule list starts with permit TCP established, then permits UDP from source ports 53 and 123 (and 7844 for a tunnel using QUIC), before the final deny
checks.fix: OVH: add, before the final deny, permit TCP with option established; permit UDP source port 53; permit UDP source port 123; and for a QUIC tunnel permit UDP source port 7844
checks.breaks: Each source port rule also lets any sender reach the host's UDP ports from that source port (see PFW-003).

checks.title: What the provider firewall allows
checks.rationale: One row per provider firewall rule, in evaluation order, so the report shows the outer layer next to the host firewall. Rule names and descriptions are not shown: they are free text and facts files are attached to bug reports.
checks.fix: Nothing to fix; this lists the rules the other PFW checks judge
